title: Why chips need test access
summary: A modern chip contains hundreds of test and debug **instruments** — MBIST controllers, logic BIST, sensors, PLL and fuse settings — but only a handful of pins are free for test. This topic explains how a few serial pins reach all of them, and which IEEE standards define the way.
objectives: Explain what an embedded instrument is and why so many need access.
Name the IEEE standards for test access and what each covers.
Explain serial access through a shift register and its cost in clock cycles.

blocks.md: An **embedded instrument** is any on-chip block that is configured, started or read for test, debug or monitoring: the MBIST controllers of the last training, logic BIST, temperature and voltage sensors, PLL settings, the fuses that store repair information, trace and debug logic. A large SoC has **hundreds** of them.

blocks.caption: Four or five test pins and a network inside the chip reach every instrument

blocks.title: The idea
blocks.md: Give every instrument a small **register** and connect the registers into **shift paths**. A tester writes and reads them bit by bit through a few pins. One access port, one protocol, any number of instruments.

rows: the **test access port** (TAP): pins, state machine, instruction and data registers; boundary-scan cells for **board** test
a standard **wrapper** around a core so it can be tested on its own inside an SoC
**networks** that connect many instruments behind the TAP, and languages to describe them (ICL) and to operate them (PDL)
boundary scan for AC-coupled high-speed links; test access for stacked 3D dies
blocks.caption: IEEE standards for test access

blocks.md: The name **JTAG** comes from the *Joint Test Action Group*, the industry group that started the work in the 1980s. Today *JTAG* is used for the TAP itself, and the same port is used for **debugging** processors and **programming** FPGAs and flash — far beyond its original purpose.

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the standards in the order they were published.

steps.title: A shift register
steps.md: Four flip-flops in a chain between **TDI** (test data in) and **TDO** (test data out). Every clock moves each bit one place on.

steps.title: Clock 1
steps.md: The first bit enters from TDI.

steps.title: Clock 2
steps.md: It moves on; the second bit follows.

steps.title: Clock 3
steps.md: Three bits are in the register.

steps.title: Clock 4
steps.md: The register holds the new value **1011**. At the same time its **old** content has come out at TDO — writing and reading happen in one pass.

blocks.title: The price: one clock per bit
blocks.md: Accessing an n-bit register takes about n clocks of the test clock. A path of 4000 bits at 10 MHz needs 0.4 ms for every access. Keeping the shift paths **short** is a central goal of the IJTAG networks in Topic 6.
